Flow matching learns a velocity field that transports a distribution of initial samples toward a data distribution.
For the action example, $A$ is a demonstrated chunk, $o$ is its observation, and $\epsilon$ is Gaussian noise of the same shape.

## Choose a path and its velocity {#flow-matching}

Use the convention $\tau=0$ for noise and $\tau=1$ for clean data.
For an independently sampled demonstration and noise, a simple straight training path is

$$
  A^\tau=(1-\tau)\epsilon+\tau A.
$$

The path's target velocity is $u=A-\epsilon$.
Training samples $\tau$, constructs $A^\tau$, and evaluates

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \hat u&=v_\theta(A^\tau,o,\tau),\\
  L_{\mathrm{flow}}&=\mathbb E[\|\hat u-u\|^2].
  \end{aligned}
$$

The target $u$ comes from the known training pair.
At inference, the target action is unavailable; the network predicts a velocity from the current sample and conditioning.
Starting at $A^0=\epsilon$, generation integrates

$$
  \frac{dA^\tau}{d\tau}=v_\theta(A^\tau,o,\tau).
$$

For example, one Euler step is

$$
  A^{\tau+\Delta\tau}
  =A^\tau+\Delta\tau\,v_\theta(A^\tau,o,\tau).
$$

The velocity is in action-space units per unit of generative time.
It is not necessarily the robot's physical joint velocity.
An action chunk can contain position commands even when the generator predicts this mathematical velocity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the target velocity and a reversed time convention"}

During construction of one training path, $A$ and $\epsilon$ are fixed.
Differentiating their interpolation gives

$$
  \frac{d}{d\tau}[(1-\tau)\epsilon+\tau A]
  =A-\epsilon.
$$

If another convention uses $s=1-\tau$, its path is $A^s=s\epsilon+(1-s)A$.
Its derivative with respect to $s$ is $\epsilon-A$.
Generation then runs from $s=1$ down to $s=0$.
Changing the time convention changes both the velocity sign and the integration direction.

:::

Straight training paths do not imply that every generated trajectory is straight.
The trained network aggregates compatible supervision into a marginal velocity field, which the solver follows.
The framework and its marginalisation result come from [Flow Matching, Section 3 and Theorems 1–2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747).

## Why local averages can preserve multiple modes {#local-averaging}

The ideal flow predictor is

$$
  v^*(x,o,\tau)
  =\mathbb E[A-\epsilon\mid A^\tau=x,o,\tau].
$$

Two samples at different locations $x$ need not receive the same velocity.
The conditional mean here describes the net movement of probability mass at one location and time.
It does not require every initial sample to end at the mean demonstrated action.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof sketch: averaging probability flux preserves the marginal path"}

Hold the observation fixed and consider smooth conditional densities $p_\tau(x\mid c)$ with velocities $u_\tau(x\mid c)$.
Here, $c$ labels a training condition with fixed mixing density $\rho(c)$.
Assume differentiation can pass under the integral and each conditional pair satisfies the continuity equation.

Define the mixture and its probability flux by

$$
  p_\tau(x)=\int p_\tau(x\mid c)\rho(c)\,dc,
$$

$$
  j_\tau(x)=
  \int p_\tau(x\mid c)u_\tau(x\mid c)\rho(c)\,dc.
$$

Integrating the conditional continuity equations gives

$$
  \partial_\tau p_\tau(x)
  +\nabla_x\cdot j_\tau(x)=0.
$$

Where $p_\tau(x)>0$, let $v_\tau(x)=j_\tau(x)/p_\tau(x)$.
This is the conditional average velocity given the location, and it yields

$$
  \partial_\tau p_\tau
  +\nabla_x\cdot(p_\tau v_\tau)=0.
$$

Thus the averaged field gives the intended marginal probability evolution under these assumptions.
This is a distribution-level result; it does not recover a unique original training pair for every generated sample.
See the full assumptions and proof in Flow Matching, Appendix A.

:::

This construction allows multimodal distributions; it does not guarantee that every trained model covers every mode.
Data imbalance, approximation error, optimisation, and inaccurate numerical integration can still remove or distort modes.
Mode averaging by a point predictor and mode dropping by a generator are distinct failure mechanisms.

## Connect the field to a sampler {#connections}

A [generative sampler](../robotics/generative-sampling.qmd) integrates the predicted field from an initial noise draw.
[Direct MSE regression](loss.qmd#conditional-mean) instead predicts one final answer for an observation.
The [flow-matching paper review](../../literature-review/theory/flow-matching.qmd) derives Gaussian conditional paths and the equality of conditional and marginal objective gradients.
[π0](../../literature-review/action/pi0.qmd) applies flow matching to observation-conditioned robot actions.
